title: Postgres Connection Pool Exhaustion on Checkout Flow
symptoms: HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout on /api/v1/checkout/pay
p99 latency spiked from 180ms to 5400ms
checkout-service active DB connections hit pool maximum 100/100
Upstream ingress queue backlog grew to 1,200 pending requests

triggers.description: Release v2.4.1 deployed 20 minutes prior with new discount eligibility logic

investigation_steps: Checked ingress gateway error logs: saw 504 Gateway Timeouts
Hypothesized high traffic overload and scaled up pod replicas
Noticed database connection count exploded and Postgres CPU pegged at 98%
Inspected pg_stat_activity for running queries
Found table lock on user_coupons table caused by missing index
Killed slow query PID 89104 and restored pool limits

actions_attempted.observable_effect: Exhausted database connection pool; worsened latency to 8.2s

actions_attempted.action_taken: Terminated blocking lock PID and capped per-pod pool connections
actions_attempted.observable_effect: Connection pool drained to 28; p99 latency normalized to 210ms in 90s

root_cause: Release v2.4.1 introduced SELECT * FROM user_coupons WHERE code = $1 FOR UPDATE without an index on 'code'. Under concurrent checkouts, queries ran full sequential table scans and held row locks for >4500ms, completely saturating the PostgreSQL connection pool.
final_resolution: Terminated blocking query PID 89104, scaled down extraneous pods, added compound index on (code, user_id), and enforced a 3s statement_timeout in the PostgreSQL connection string.
lessons_learned: Never scale out pods during database connection pool saturation.
Enforce statement_timeout on all currency calculation queries.
Add compound index on table row locks before deployment.

title: Redis Cache Stampede & Replica Saturation During Flash Sale
symptoms: HTTP 500 Internal Server Error rate 18.2% on /api/v1/inventory/stock
Redis cluster CPU utilization spiked to 99.4%
MySQL read replica replication lag spiked from 2ms to 42 seconds
Catalog stock status displaying 'Out of Stock' incorrectly to shoppers

triggers.description: Flash sale notification push sent to 450,000 mobile app users at 14:00 UTC

investigation_steps: Received alert on Redis CPU > 95%
Observed thousands of concurrent requests querying item stock for 3 trending flash-sale SKUs
Identified that cache key expired simultaneously for all 3 hot items
Implemented single-flight cache mutex and TTL jitter

actions_attempted.action_taken: Executed FLUSHDB on degraded Redis cache node to purge corrupted cache
actions_attempted.hypothesis: Believed Redis cache memory fragmentation or corrupted keys caused high CPU
actions_attempted.observable_effect: Flushing cache dumped 100% of read traffic directly onto MySQL database, crashing the read replica instantly

actions_attempted.action_taken: Applied emergency hotfix enabling singleflight request coalescing in inventory-service
actions_attempted.hypothesis: Ensure only 1 backend query hits database per cache miss, while concurrent requests await same promise
actions_attempted.observable_effect: MySQL query rate for hot SKUs plummeted from 14,000 QPS to 1 QPS; replica lag recovered in 3 minutes

root_cause: The top 3 flash sale SKUs were cached with fixed 300s TTL without randomized jitter. When the TTL expired at 14:05 UTC during peak traffic, 14,000 concurrent requests simultaneously missed cache and pounded the underlying MySQL read replica (thundering herd problem).
final_resolution: Implemented singleflight request coalescing in the Go inventory service and injected randomized TTL jitter (+/- 25%) on all cache writes.
lessons_learned: CRITICAL ANTI-PATTERN: Never run FLUSHDB or flush cache clusters during high traffic spikes; it creates an immediate catastrophic database overload.
All cache keys for high-cardinality promotion items must employ TTL jitter and singleflight coalescing.
Configure circuit breakers between cache layer and MySQL read replica.
runbook_recommendations: Monitor read replica thread pool status: SHOW PROCESSLIST;

title: Authentication Gateway Lockup due to Uncached External JWKS Fetch
symptoms: HTTP 401 Unauthorized spikes on 92% of inbound API requests across all services
auth-service response latency exceeded 10,000ms
All downstream microservices failing token verification
auth-service container memory steadily climbed until OOMKilled

triggers.description: Third-party Identity Provider (Auth0) reported degraded latency in EU region

investigation_steps: Noticed global 401 cascade across all frontends
Restarted auth-service pods, which failed health check startup probes
Traced outbound network calls from auth-service
Identified auth-service making synchronous HTTPS GET to Auth0 /.well-known/jwks.json on every incoming request

actions_attempted.action_taken: Restarted auth-service deployment via kubectl rollout restart
actions_attempted.hypothesis: Clear memory leak and reset stuck HTTP connections
actions_attempted.observable_effect: New pods were unable to pass readiness probes because external IdP endpoint was timing out; entered CrashLoopBackOff

actions_attempted.action_taken: Configured local in-memory JWKS public key cache with 24-hour TTL and fallback to last known valid keys
actions_attempted.hypothesis: Eliminate synchronous external network dependency during token validation
actions_attempted.observable_effect: Auth verification latency dropped to 1.8ms; error rate returned to 0% immediately

root_cause: The JWT validation library had its in-memory key cache disabled due to an incorrect configuration flag in a recent config update. Every inbound API request initiated an outbound HTTPS call to download JWKS public keys. When the external IdP experienced latency, all auth worker threads hung.
final_resolution: Enabled local persistent in-memory caching for JWKS public keys with stale-while-revalidate and a 24-hour local expiration.
lessons_learned: Never allow synchronous outbound external HTTP dependencies in critical authentication request path.
Readiness probes must never depend on third-party external networks or external IdP availability.
Public signing keys change rarely; cache them persistently with graceful degradation.
runbook_recommendations: Verify JWKS cache status via: curl -s http://localhost:8080/internal/jwks-cache/status
Verify egress connectivity to IdP: curl -I -m 2 https://auth.company.com/.well-known/jwks.json

title: Payment Webhook Thread Starvation & Queue Congestion
symptoms: Stripe payment confirmations delayed by up to 2 hours
Stripe automated webhook delivery reporting 503 Service Unavailable
Pending webhook queue backlog exceeded 48,000 events
Customers reporting completed card charges but unfulfilled digital orders

triggers.description: Monthly subscription billing run triggered 50,000 webhook events simultaneously

investigation_steps: Observed Stripe webhook endpoint 503 error alerts
Checked Celery worker queue metrics: saw massive backlog
Discovered synchronous accounting ledger API calls inside the HTTP webhook handler

actions_attempted.action_taken: Increased Gunicorn synchronous HTTP worker threads from 16 to 128
actions_attempted.hypothesis: Allow more concurrent incoming webhook connections to prevent 503 errors
actions_attempted.observable_effect: Memory usage surged to 100%; Linux kernel OOM killer started killing Gunicorn processes continuously

actions_attempted.action_taken: Refactored webhook endpoint to return HTTP 200 immediately after pushing raw payload into Redis queue
actions_attempted.hypothesis: Decouple synchronous HTTP acknowledgment from asynchronous ledger reconciliation
actions_attempted.observable_effect: HTTP webhook response dropped to 8ms; Stripe stopped retrying; queue backlog cleared in 18 minutes

root_cause: The webhook handler performed synchronous external ERP ledger reconciliation and PDF receipt generation before returning HTTP 200 to Stripe. When batch billing fired 50,000 events, worker threads starved and Stripe began exponential retries, multiplying traffic by 4x.
final_resolution: Decoupled webhook ingestion from business processing: handlers now write raw payloads into an async queue and acknowledge with HTTP 200 immediately within <15ms.
lessons_learned: CRITICAL RULE: Webhook endpoints must never perform synchronous business processing or external network calls before acknowledging receipt.
Avoid inflating synchronous worker threads to handle backlogs; convert to async event queues instead.
runbook_recommendations: Inspect webhook queue depth: redis-cli LLEN queues:payment_webhooks
Check Stripe webhook event delivery dashboard for 5xx retry rates.

title: P99 Latency Surge & 504 Timeouts on Checkout API Post-Release
symptoms: HTTP 504 Gateway Timeouts rising rapidly on /api/v1/checkout/finalize
checkout-service p99 latency spiked from 195ms to 4900ms
Postgres connection pool queue count steadily growing (currently 88/100 active connections)
Customer cart abandonments up 340% in last 15 minutes

triggers.description: Release v2.4.5 deployed 14 minutes ago with new multi-currency checkout calculation

investigation_steps: Alert triggered on PagerDuty: checkout-service high latency and 504 rates
Incident room opened in Slack #incident-20260928-checkout
Engineer reviewing telemetry and checking if previous similar incidents occurred

actions_attempted.observable_effect: Exhausted database connection pool; worsened latency to 8.2s

actions_attempted.action_taken: Terminated blocking lock PID and capped per-pod pool connections
actions_attempted.observable_effect: Connection pool drained to 22%; p99 latency normalized to 210ms in 90s

root_cause: Release v2.4.5 multi-currency calculation held exclusive row locks on exchange_rates table without compound index.
final_resolution: Terminated query PID 91204, added migration index on (currency, effective_date), and adjusted statement_timeout to 3s.
lessons_learned: Never scale out pods during database connection pool saturation.
Enforce statement_timeout on all currency calculation queries.
Add compound index on table row locks before deployment.
